questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.stem: A clinician compares two patients with the same diagnosis and the same treatment, one of whom recovered and one of whom did not. What makes this comparison controlled rather than merely a pair of cases placed side by side?

options.text: The two cases share the features the clinician says matter, so a difference in outcome is worth asking about.
The two cases have different outcomes, which gives the comparison something to explain.
options.misconception: treats the difference in outcome as the source of control

options.text: The two cases are described at length, so the reader can judge them for themselves.
options.misconception: confuses detail of description with similarity of design

options.text: The two cases came from the same clinic, so the clinician controls for the local setting.
options.misconception: treats a shared location as the only thing control requires

questions.explanation: A comparison is controlled when the cases are alike in the respects the investigator claims to hold constant. Different outcomes supply the question, not the control.
questions.hint: Ask what result could show the two cases were unlike.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a note must add to become a comparison
questions.stem: A clinician's note places two patients side by side without any attempt to hold anything constant. In two or three sentences, explain what is missing before the note could be called a comparison.

answer.exemplar: The note needs to say which features of the two cases are being treated as alike, since without that the reader cannot tell whether the outcome difference reflects the patients or the care. It also needs a stated reason for pairing these two patients in particular, because a juxtaposition chosen for interest rather than for comparison carries no evidential weight at all.

questions.explanation: A juxtaposition is two cases placed near each other, while a comparison holds selected features constant and says so. Without that statement, a reader cannot tell what the pairing was meant to show.
questions.hint: Say which features are the same in both cases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Identify the variable that is not measured the same way in a pair

stimulus.body: Patient A, admitted with community acquired pneumonia, received four days of intravenous antibiotics. Patient B, admitted with the same diagnosis twelve months earlier, received eight days of intravenous antibiotics with the same agents.

questions.stem: Which aspect of this comparison is not controlled?

options.text: The duration of antibiotic treatment differs between the two cases.
The two patients share the same diagnosis and the same antibiotic agents.
options.misconception: ignores a feature that is genuinely held constant

options.text: The two patients were admitted to the same ward of the same hospital.
options.misconception: misses the variation that is actually present

options.text: The two cases are recorded in the same file with the same identifiers and format.
options.misconception: treats record-keeping as part of the clinical comparison

questions.explanation: A variable that differs between the cases is the candidate explanation for the outcome difference, and here treatment duration is exactly that. Sharing diagnosis and ward says nothing about the care.
questions.hint: Look for what differs between the two descriptions.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: Read a contextual difference as a candidate explanation
questions.stem: Two patients with the same condition recover at different speeds, and the clinician notes that one worked while the other did not. What is the most defensible reading?

options.text: Work explains the difference, since the clinician noticed it and recorded it in the note.
options.misconception: treats a recorded observation as a demonstrated cause

options.text: The difference cannot be explained at all, because two cases can never support any conclusion.
options.misconception: denies that a comparison can carry any inference

options.text: The difference is due to the condition's severity, which the note records as differing.
options.misconception: assumes the note identifies a cause it merely describes

options.text: Work is a contextual difference to consider, not a cause that the note establishes.

questions.explanation: A feature that differs between the cases is a candidate explanation, and the note records it without testing it. Treating it as a cause adds more than the evidence supports.
questions.hint: Ask whether the note tested the difference it noticed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claiming a mechanism and testing it elsewhere
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether a mechanism travels to another setting
questions.stem: A clinician argues that early physiotherapy reduces readmission after hip surgery, based on two wards. Which step would test whether the mechanism travels elsewhere?

options.text: Repeat the same two wards with more patients, which confirms the result in place.
options.misconception: mistakes more of the same cases for a test of transfer

options.text: Ask patients at another hospital whether physiotherapy helped them personally.
options.misconception: substitutes recollection for a comparison that could test it

options.text: Compare an early physiotherapy ward with a similar ward elsewhere that introduced it later.
Publish the two ward results and let other hospitals draw their own conclusions.
options.misconception: leaves the transfer question to whoever reads the paper

questions.explanation: A mechanism claim travels only if it can be shown elsewhere under similar conditions. Re-running the same wards tests size, and patient recollection tests belief.
questions.hint: Look for a similar setting that has not yet been tested.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When a finding may be carried to another context
questions.learningObjective: State the conditions under which a finding may be carried across
questions.stem: A clinician finds that a discharge checklist reduced readmissions in one hospital trust. Which judgement about carrying the finding to another trust is most defensible?

options.text: It can be carried if the other trust has comparable conditions and the same measurement of readmission.
It can be carried to any trust, because a checklist is simple and any staff can apply it.
options.misconception: confuses ease of adoption with similarity of conditions

options.text: It cannot be carried, because findings never apply outside the place where they were made.
options.misconception: denies that any generalisation is ever justified

options.text: It can be carried if the second trust believes the checklist is a good idea.
options.misconception: treats belief in the practice as a condition for transfer

questions.explanation: A finding travels when the new setting resembles the old in the conditions that produced it and measures the outcome the same way. Simplicity of the intervention does not decide it.
questions.hint: Ask how similar the second setting is and how it measures.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: One concept, two words, two sets of cases
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a term carrying two different meanings
questions.stem: Two papers use the word recovery for different things, one meaning symptom remission and the other meaning return to independent living. In two or three sentences, explain what this does to a comparison between the two.

answer.exemplar: The comparison becomes a comparison of two different measures unless the writer says which meaning is in play on each side. Two services can both report high recovery rates while counting entirely different things, so a case for one over the other cannot be made from the figures until the terms are aligned.

questions.explanation: When a term carries different meanings in the two sets of cases, the numbers are not measuring the same thing. Until the definitions are aligned, the comparison rests on a mismatch.
questions.hint: Check what each side counts as recovery.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two fields counting at different levels
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a comparison built on different denominators
questions.stem: An audit compares a surgical ward that counts complications per hundred operations with a medical ward that counts complications per thousand bed days. What is the problem with the comparison?

options.text: Both wards should count complications per operation, because operations are the standard unit.
options.misconception: prescribes one unit for a ward with no operations

options.text: The ward with the lower figure has better care, since raw counts favour larger units.
options.misconception: reads raw counts as though they were comparable rates

options.text: The denominators differ, so the two figures do not describe the same quantity.
Complications cannot be counted accurately in either ward, so the comparison is impossible.
options.misconception: declares the whole task impossible, not just the comparison

questions.explanation: Rates built on different denominators describe different quantities, so placing them side by side compares nothing. Declaring counting impossible avoids the smaller task of a common basis.
questions.hint: Ask what each denominator makes the figure a measure of.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: Specify what would make a proportion comparison controlled
questions.stem: A clinician compares two clinics on the proportion of patients reviewed within two weeks. What detail would make this comparison controlled?

options.text: A statement that both clinics use the same definition of review and the same clock for starting it.
A statement that both clinics have the same number of consultants on the team.
options.misconception: supplies a detail that does not bear on the measured outcome

options.text: A statement that both clinics received the same number of patients in the year.
options.misconception: tries to control a variable the measure does not depend on

options.text: A statement that the larger clinic has been open longer than the smaller one.
options.misconception: records a background fact unconnected to the measure

questions.explanation: Control means holding constant what could change the measured outcome, here the definition of review and when the clock starts. Staffing and patient volume matter only if they alter the proportion.
questions.hint: Ask what could change the figure other than the care.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Classify a note as juxtaposition or comparison
questions.stem: A clinician notes two similar cases side by side without saying why they were paired. Which judgement about this note is most accurate?

options.text: The note is a comparison, because placing two similar cases together is the definition of one.
options.misconception: treats adjacency as a method in itself

options.text: The note is a comparison, because the cases were similar in every respect the note records.
options.misconception: assumes similarity of record establishes control

options.text: The note is a juxtaposition, because it does not state what was held constant or why.
The note cannot be assessed, since a reader may never know what the clinician had in mind.
options.misconception: calls the note unassessable when it is merely incomplete

questions.explanation: A comparison states which features are held constant and why the pair was chosen. A note that gives neither is a juxtaposition, and reading the writer's mind is not the reader's job.
questions.hint: Ask what the note says about what was held constant.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a variable measured inconsistently across two cases
questions.stem: A clinician compares two services using the phrase length of stay, one measured to discharge from the ward and the other to discharge from the hospital. What does this show?

options.text: That the two services differ in quality, since a shorter stay is always a better outcome.
options.misconception: treats a measurement mismatch as a quality finding

options.text: That the two services should agree a common definition before the data are published.
options.misconception: prescribes a fix without naming the fault in the comparison

options.text: That the service measuring to hospital discharge must be the one with longer stays.
options.misconception: infers a direction of difference from a mismatch alone

options.text: That the variable was not measured the same way in the two cases, so the figures are not comparable.

questions.explanation: Two figures built on different endpoints do not describe the same quantity, so their difference says nothing about the services. Quality judgements assume a comparability not provided.
questions.hint: Ask whether both figures count the same thing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a recorded difference from an established cause
questions.stem: Two comparable patients with the same infection recover at very different rates, and the note records that one received the antibiotic sooner. In two or three sentences, explain what the note can and cannot support.

answer.exemplar: The note supports the observation that the two cases differed in how quickly treatment began, and it gives a reason to consider that timing in future comparisons. It cannot support a claim that timing caused the difference in outcome, because two cases cannot exclude other explanations, and a note that stops at the observation leaves the question open rather than answering it.

questions.explanation: A record of a difference is a starting point for explanation, not its conclusion. Attributing the outcome to it requires more than noting that it differed.
questions.hint: Ask whether cause is recorded or only difference.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claiming a mechanism and testing it elsewhere
questions.learningObjective: Separate two simultaneous changes in a service evaluation

stimulus.body: Note on a ward: since the introduction of twice-weekly physiotherapy for patients after knee replacement, the average time to independent walking has fallen from nine days to six. The ward has also changed its discharge planning meeting to the same day each week.

questions.stem: Which change would best test whether the improvement came from the physiotherapy?

options.text: Compare the nine-day figure with the figure from the two years before the change was introduced.
options.misconception: extends the same period rather than adding a comparison

options.text: Ask the physiotherapy staff why they believe the change has worked so well.
options.misconception: substitutes the staff's confidence for a test

options.text: Compare the same ward's outcomes before and after a different discharge meeting was introduced.
Record the improvement in the annual report so that other wards can see the figure.
options.misconception: treats publication as evidence that the mechanism holds

questions.explanation: The physiotherapy and the discharge meeting changed together, so the note cannot separate them. Introducing the change at a different time offers the comparison that could isolate it.
questions.hint: Two things changed at once, so vary one of them.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When a finding may be carried to another context
questions.learningObjective: Specify the checks needed before carrying a finding across
questions.stem: A clinic's fall in emergency readmissions after a new triage protocol is being cited by another trust. Which check should that trust make before adopting it?

options.text: Compare the two trusts' patients, staffing and readmission definition, and see whether the conditions match.
Check that the protocol is written clearly enough for staff to follow without training.
options.misconception: treats implementation ease as the condition for transfer

options.text: Check whether the first trust has published the figures, since published results are more reliable.
options.misconception: treats publication status as evidence of validity

options.text: Check whether the first trust's patients are similar, since the patients explain the results.
options.misconception: considers only one of the conditions that would matter

questions.explanation: Transfer requires that the conditions which produced the result are present in the new setting and that both measure readmission the same way. Clarity of the protocol captures only part of that.
questions.hint: Compare conditions and measures, not just the protocol.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: One concept, two words, two sets of cases
questions.learningObjective: Identify the definition check needed before comparing two percentages
questions.stem: Two services both report a high percentage of patients discharged with a care plan in place. What should the reader check before comparing the two percentages?

options.text: That both services used the same survey method to ask the question.
options.misconception: focuses on method while ignoring the term itself

options.text: That both services recorded the discharges within the same reporting period.
options.misconception: checks timing but not what the figure counts

options.text: That the services were inspected in the same year and by the same body.
options.misconception: checks the inspecting body rather than the counted thing

options.text: That both services count a care plan the same way before reading anything into the figures.

questions.explanation: Before two percentages can be compared, the thing each counts has to be the same, since services differ in what they accept as a care plan. Method and timing come after that.
questions.hint: Check what each side counts as a care plan.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two fields counting at different levels
questions.learningObjective: Identify the denominator fault in a rate comparison
questions.stem: A comparison sets a hospital's complications per thousand discharges beside a ward's complications per hundred patients. What is the main fault in the comparison?

options.text: The figures should be ordered so that the smaller number comes first, to avoid emphasis.
options.misconception: treats presentation order as an evidential problem

options.text: Neither figure is reliable, because complications are recorded differently in every unit.
options.misconception: declares counting unreliable instead of rebuilding a basis

options.text: The hospital figure should be excluded, since wards are the smaller unit of care.
options.misconception: excludes data by unit rather than by comparability

options.text: The rates count over different denominators, so they are not measuring the same thing.

questions.explanation: Two rates with different denominators are two different quantities, and the order in which they are printed cannot fix that. Excluding one side abandons the comparison rather than repairing it.
questions.hint: Ask what each denominator makes the figure a measure of.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a comparison controlled rather than accidental
questions.stem: A clinician compares two ward rounds that both produce a satisfaction score for patients. In two or three sentences, explain what would make the comparison controlled rather than accidental.

answer.exemplar: The comparison would need to say what was made identical between the two rounds, such as the questions asked, when they were asked and by whom, and the ward conditions that might shape the answers. Two scores are comparable only when the reader knows the same thing was measured in the same way on both sides, otherwise the gap may reflect the instrument rather than the care.

questions.explanation: Control is a statement about what was held constant, so a comparison must declare the constants that matter to the measurement. Otherwise a difference in asking is mistaken for a difference in care.
questions.hint: Ask what was measured in the same way on both sides.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Identify the uncontrolled variable in a ward round comparison

stimulus.body: Note: compared with the patients treated on the old ward round, patients treated on the new ward round were seen sooner after admission and had fewer unplanned transfers. Both groups were admitted during the same six months.

questions.stem: What is the strongest objection to calling this a controlled comparison?

options.text: It is not controlled because the two groups were treated in the same six months.
options.misconception: treats a shared period as evidence against control

options.text: It is not controlled because the note does not say how many patients were in each group.
options.misconception: complains about a missing count, not a missing control

options.text: One visible difference between the groups, time to first review, may explain the outcomes.
It is not controlled because a ward round cannot ever be compared with another ward round.
options.misconception: rules out the comparison on kind rather than on design

questions.explanation: The two groups differ in when they were first seen, and that difference could account for the outcome gap on its own. A shared period does not remove a variable left free to vary.
questions.hint: Look for a difference between the groups that stayed free.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Put two measurements on a common basis
questions.stem: A clinician compares outcomes of two clinics, one recording blood pressure in millimetres of mercury and the other in kilopascals. Which correction is best?

options.text: Convert only the clinic with the larger number so that the two figures look similar.
options.misconception: adjusts a figure to flatter a comparison

options.text: Convert both to the same unit and state the unit and the measurement method for each.
Report both figures in their original units and let readers convert them themselves.
options.misconception: pushes the conversion work onto the reader

options.text: Use whichever unit the wider readership prefers, since the numbers do not really differ.
options.misconception: picks a unit by audience rather than for comparability

questions.explanation: Two measurements of the same quantity in different units can be compared once both are expressed in one unit, provided the reader is told what each was. Converting one to look similar obscures it.
questions.hint: Put both on one unit and say what each was measured in.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: Move from a noticed difference to a testable explanation
questions.stem: Two comparable patients admitted with the same condition had very different lengths of stay, and the note records that one had a longer wait for a specialist opinion. What is the strongest next step?

options.text: Conclude that waiting for specialist opinions lengthens stays and record it as the cause.
options.misconception: treats a recorded difference as an established cause

options.text: Discard the comparison, since one differing feature makes the two cases useless.
options.misconception: discards a usable pair over one uncontrolled variable

options.text: Reread the note to check that the two lengths of stay were calculated in the same way.
options.misconception: checks the wrong stage of the problem

options.text: Compare the waiting times against length of stay across more patients with the condition.

questions.explanation: A difference noticed in two cases becomes a candidate explanation that can be tested with more cases, where waiting time varies against outcome. Concluding from the pair misses that step.
questions.hint: Test the candidate explanation across more cases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claiming a mechanism and testing it elsewhere
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of a proposed mechanism
questions.stem: A clinician claims that a falls-prevention programme works because it builds confidence in walking. Which further evidence would test that mechanism rather than the programme?

options.text: A larger sample of patients completing the programme, which strengthens the claim directly.
options.misconception: adds numbers without testing the proposed mechanism

options.text: A longer follow-up period, which would show whether the effect persists over time.
options.misconception: tests durability rather than the proposed mechanism

options.text: Whether patients who gained confidence but did not attend the programme also fell less often.
A satisfaction survey of participants, which would show the programme is valued.
options.misconception: measures appreciation rather than the mechanism

questions.explanation: A mechanism claim is tested by separating the proposed ingredient from the package. If confidence is what works, people who gained it by other means should show the same effect.
questions.hint: Separate the proposed ingredient from the whole package.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When a finding may be carried to another context
questions.learningObjective: Explain the preconditions for carrying a finding to a new setting
questions.stem: A clinician wants to apply a finding about a community rehabilitation service to a hospital ward. In two or three sentences, explain what must be checked before the finding is carried across.

answer.exemplar: The two settings differ in what the finding depended on, so the clinician must check that the hospital ward has the same staffing, the same patient mix and the same room for the routines that made the community service work. It also matters whether the outcome is measured the same way, because a service that counts independent living and a ward that counts discharge without support are not counting the same thing.

questions.explanation: A finding carries across when the conditions that produced it are present in the new setting and the outcome is measured comparably. Moving it without checking transports the label, not the effect.
questions.hint: Compare the conditions and the outcome measure.

options.misconception: treats a shared label as a shared measurement

options.text: The first service has a problem, because it starts the clock earlier than the other.
options.misconception: judges the service by the choice of starting point

options.text: The figures count different intervals, so they cannot be compared as they stand.

questions.explanation: Two waiting times can share a name and still count different intervals, and the gap between them comes from where each clock starts. Ranking the services on such figures would mislead.

questions.stem: A service reports falls per thousand bed days and a ward reports falls per hundred patients. Which step would let the two be compared properly?

options.misconception: identifies a possible confounder but not the definition

options.text: Were the two teams assessed in the same year and by the same inspector?
options.misconception: fixes on inspection rather than on measurement

questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Classify a pairing that states no design
questions.stem: A clinician's notes place two patients with the same diagnosis under each other, one of whom had a longer admission. What distinguishes this from a comparison?

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them, since placing cases together is the standard method of comparison.
options.misconception: denies that method and evidence differ

options.text: It is a comparison, because the two patients are similar enough to be worth placing together.
options.misconception: confuses similarity of subjects with control of variables

options.text: It is a juxtaposition, since it does not state what is held constant or what the pairing is for.
It is not a comparison, because the two patients differ in the length of their admission.
options.misconception: rejects a comparison on a reason every comparison allows

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of different instruments shows
questions.stem: A clinician finds that two teams use different pain score scales and compares their average scores. In two or three sentences, explain what the comparison actually shows.

answer.exemplar: The two averages describe two different instruments, so their difference says more about the scales than about the care the patients received. A reader cannot tell whether one team relieved more pain, and the note should say so, because the practice of comparing scores from different instruments is the source of the apparent difference rather than the patients' experience.

questions.explanation: An average is meaningless without knowing what was averaged and how it was scored. Comparing figures produced by different instruments transfers the difference in the instruments onto the patients.
questions.hint: Ask what was measured and with what instrument.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: State what a two-patient note can safely conclude

stimulus.body: Two patients were admitted with the same exacerbation of asthma on the same night. One was treated on the ward and the other was treated in the observation area for six hours before admission, and the ward patient's stay was a day shorter.

questions.stem: What can the note safely conclude from this comparison?

options.text: Very little about the treatments, since the patients differed before admission.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the difficulty of comparing rates over different populations
questions.stem: A clinician compares a community service counting episodes per thousand residents with a hospital counting episodes per thousand discharges. In two or three sentences, explain the difficulty with this comparison.

answer.exemplar: The two rates have different populations in their denominators, so the community figure describes events per head of population while the hospital figure describes events per group of discharges. options.misconception: reads incomparable rates as a performance ranking

options.misconception: turns a single observed difference into a causal claim

options.text: Treat the timing of physiotherapy as a candidate explanation and gather cases that vary on it.
Add a note that the two patients differed in ways the record does not capture.
options.misconception: adds a caution without any plan to test the explanation

options.text: Remove the note, since a comparison of two patients proves nothing and should not be kept.
options.misconception: discards the record on the ground that it is not proof

answer.exemplar: The clinician could compare wards where a plan is recorded but no checklist is used, against wards using the checklist, and ask whether the recording alone accounts for any difference. options.misconception: asks for more time in the old setting, not a comparison

options.misconception: denies that any transfer is ever defensible

options.text: The new setting differs in population and in discharge process, so the result may not hold there.
The extension is sound, because home-based rehabilitation is already known to work well in cities.
options.misconception: borrows an unsupported generalisation to justify transfer

questions.explanation: Transfer depends on whether the conditions behind the result are reproduced in the new setting, and here population and discharge process differ. Waiting longer in the old setting misses it.
questions.hint: Ask what the original result depended on.

answer.exemplar: The note would need to state which features the cases share and which vary, and then show that the outcome tracked the varying feature rather than the shared ones. options.text: Check whether the two services served comparable numbers of patients in the same year.
options.misconception: checks volume and year before the definition of the plan

options.text: Check whether the hospital's figure was reported to the national body last year.
options.misconception: leans on an external reporting habit for evidential weight

options.text: Check whether both count a care plan the same way before comparing anything.

questions.explanation: Two percentages cannot be compared until the counted category is the same on both sides, so the definition comes first. Collection method and reporting habits fix no mismatch in what was counted.
questions.hint: Check the definition of the counted thing first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two fields counting at different levels
questions.learningObjective: Judge a comparison of rates over different populations
questions.stem: A clinician compares a hospital's readmissions per thousand discharges with a community service's readmissions per thousand residents. Which judgement is correct?

options.text: The comparison is sound, because both figures are expressed per thousand.
options.misconception: treats a shared unit of scale as a shared measure

options.text: The comparison is unsound, because the denominators describe different populations at risk.
The community figure is higher, so the community service is performing worse than the hospital.
options.misconception: reads incomparable rates as a ranking of services

options.text: The hospital figure should be excluded, since discharges are not a measure of population.
options.misconception: dismisses one measure instead of aligning the two

questions.explanation: The two rates describe different populations, so the gap reflects who was counted rather than how the services performed. A shared unit of scale or a ranking avoids a common denominator.
questions.hint: Ask who is in each denominator.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a controlled comparison of an intervention requires
questions.stem: A clinician wants to know whether a longer appointment slot improves the control of blood pressure. In two or three sentences, explain what a controlled comparison would require.

answer.exemplar: The comparison would require clinics that differ in appointment length while keeping the patients, the staff, the measurement and the follow-up the same, with control of blood pressure read the same way in both. A before and after comparison within one clinic would not do, because patients, staff and season all change with it, and any improvement would be impossible to attribute to the slots.

questions.explanation: Control requires holding everything else steady while one feature varies, or comparing two settings that differ in that feature alone. A single clinic over time changes too much at once.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed alongside the appointment length.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: Classify unanalysed entries as juxtaposition

stimulus.body: A note lists a case where a patient improved after a change of ward and a case where a patient improved despite a change of ward. The writer draws no conclusion from the pair.

questions.stem: What is the most defensible reading of these two entries?

options.text: The two entries show that ward changes have no effect, since both patients improved either way.
options.misconception: reads a pattern into two entries that cannot support one

options.text: The two entries prove that clinical outcomes depend on factors other than the ward.
options.misconception: infers a general claim from a deliberately unanalysed pair

options.text: The two entries are a juxtaposition that records outcomes without comparing anything.
The two entries are a weak comparison, since the two patients at least shared the diagnosis.
options.misconception: credits a shared diagnosis as though it were a stated design

questions.explanation: Entries recorded side by side without a statement of what was held constant are a juxtaposition, and neither can carry a general claim. Calling it a weak comparison credits a design it never had.
questions.hint: Ask what the note says was being compared.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: Align two different measures of the same concept
questions.stem: Two pharmacies count adherence as tablets dispensed over the prescription period, while a ward counts it as the proportion of doses taken at the bedside. Which correction is best?

options.text: Compare the two directly, since both are proportions of medicines not taken or missed.
options.misconception: treats similar wording as a shared measurement

options.text: Recalculate both on one definition of adherence and state the period and the source of each count.
Use the pharmacy figure, since dispensing data are easier to collect and less biased.
options.misconception: prefers the easier measure rather than the comparable one

options.text: Report the two as separate indicators and leave any comparison to future work.
options.misconception: defers the comparison the note is being written to support

questions.explanation: Adherence measured from dispensing and from bedside observation are different quantities, so the two must be restated on one definition. Comparing them directly leaves the mismatch in place.
questions.hint: Restate both on one definition of adherence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: Choose the next step when a treatment differs between two cases
questions.stem: Two patients who share a condition, seen in the same week by the same consultant, had very different recoveries. The note records that one was given an antibiotic course of fourteen days and the other seven. What should the note do?

options.text: Conclude that longer antibiotic courses produce better recovery in this condition.
options.misconception: generalises a causal claim from two unmatched cases

options.text: Record the difference but note that no conclusion can be drawn from a single pair.
options.misconception: treats the note as unable to contribute any next step

options.text: Remove the antibiotic detail, since treatment differences muddy an otherwise clean comparison.
options.misconception: removes the interesting variable instead of examining it

options.text: Treat the course length as a candidate explanation and compare more cases that vary in it.

questions.explanation: A difference in treatment between two otherwise similar cases is a lead worth pursuing, and the note can carry it without claiming the outcome was caused by it. Concluding discards the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what more cases would test the treatment difference.
